title: Major trauma: primary survey and tension pneumothorax

header.contentArea: Applied surgical science and critical care

related.why: Cervical spine and head injury in the same patient
Another primary survey with its own priorities

brief.role: Core surgical trainee on the trauma team
brief.scenario: Mr Jordan Hale, 34, came off his motorcycle at speed 40 minutes ago. He is on a scoop with a collar and head blocks. He is agitated and breathless. Pulse 132, BP 78/44, RR 36, SpO2 86% on 15 L oxygen by reservoir mask.
brief.task: The trauma team leader, an emergency medicine consultant trained in thoracostomy, is present. You will not perform procedures; the examiner will ask how you would assess and manage him, giving findings as you ask.

beforeYouWalkIn.frame: A shocked, hypoxic trauma patient: work <C>ABCDE and treat each problem as you find it.
beforeYouWalkIn.trap: Sending him for a chest X-ray before decompressing a clinical tension pneumothorax.
beforeYouWalkIn.firstMove: "Catastrophic haemorrhage, then airway with the cervical spine held in line."

grid.label: Primary survey with spinal control (safety-critical)
grid.fail: Starts with the chest or removes the head blocks to look at the neck.
grid.pass: Uses <C>ABCDE: catastrophic haemorrhage, then airway with manual in-line cervical spine immobilisation, breathing, circulation, disability, exposure.
grid.high: Keeps manual in-line stabilisation during any airway intervention, and treats each problem as found before moving on.

grid.label: Recognising tension pneumothorax
grid.fail: Asks for a chest X-ray to confirm it.
grid.pass: Diagnoses it clinically: hypoxia, shock, absent breath sounds and hyper-resonance on one side; decompresses before imaging because he is unstable.
grid.high: Knows tracheal deviation and distended neck veins are late or unreliable, and hypotension is late; won't wait for them.

grid.label: Decompression site (safety-critical)
grid.fail: Can't name a site, or picks one that would injure the heart or great vessels.
grid.borderline: Uses the 2nd intercostal space, mid-clavicular line, without knowing the cannula may not reach the pleura.
grid.pass: Adult site: 4th or 5th intercostal space, just anterior to the mid-axillary line, above the rib below.
grid.high: Decompresses without delay: open thoracostomy then drain where expertise is available; needle if that can't be done immediately. Knows a 2nd-space cannula may not reach.

grid.label: Chest drain and reassessment
grid.fail: Decompresses and moves on without a drain.
grid.pass: Follows decompression with a chest drain through the thoracostomy; reassesses breathing and circulation.
grid.high: Watches for recurrence of tension, and for a large blood loss from the drain signalling haemothorax and theatre.

grid.label: Haemorrhage control and tranexamic acid
grid.fail: Gives litres of crystalloid and no tranexamic acid.
grid.pass: IV tranexamic acid as soon as possible, within 3 hours of injury; major haemorrhage protocol; blood products, not crystalloid.
grid.high: Plasma to red cells 1:1; restrictive volume, titrated to keep a central circulation, until bleeding is controlled.

grid.label: Imaging and definitive control
grid.fail: Sends an unstable, non-responding patient to CT.
grid.pass: Whole-body CT if he responds to resuscitation; if not, minimal imaging and straight to damage control surgery.
grid.high: Limits imaging to what directs intervention in a non-responder, and knows a negative FAST doesn't exclude abdominal bleeding.

grid.label: Team, leadership and escalation
grid.fail: Works alone and doesn't say findings aloud.
grid.pass: Reports each finding to the trauma team leader; calls for senior help and the consultant early.
grid.high: Gives a closed-loop summary: findings, interventions, response, and a clear next step with the teams needed.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: I'd look at his chest first, and take the collar and blocks off to feel his neck properly.

fail.speaker: examiner
fail.text: Absent breath sounds on the right, hyper-resonant, BP 78/44.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: I'd get a portable chest X-ray to confirm a pneumothorax.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: Somewhere on the front of the chest, maybe near the sternum.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: That's fixed, so I'd move on to circulation.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: No one yet; I'll update the team once the scan's done.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: <C>ABCDE. Any catastrophic bleeding first, then the airway with his cervical spine held in line manually, then breathing, circulation, disability and exposure.

pass.speaker: examiner
pass.text: Absent breath sounds on the right, hyper-resonant, BP 78/44.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: That's a tension pneumothorax. He's unstable, so I decompress now, before any X-ray.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: 4th or 5th intercostal space, just in front of the mid-axillary line, going over the top of the rib below.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: A chest drain through the same site, and reassess his breathing and circulation.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Activate the major haemorrhage protocol. Tranexamic acid now; he's within 3 hours. Blood products, not crystalloid.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: If he responds, whole-body CT. If he doesn't, he needs damage control surgery, not the scanner.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: I'd tell the trauma team leader each finding as I go and ask for the consultant early.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: <C>ABCDE, treating as I go. No catastrophic bleeding. Talking, so airway patent; someone holds his head in line manually throughout, especially if anaesthesia need to intervene.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: Absent breath sounds on the right, hyper-resonant, BP 78/44.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Right tension pneumothorax: hypoxic, shocked, with one-sided signs. I won't wait for a deviated trachea or distended neck veins; they're late and often absent, especially if he's bleeding. Decompress now, image later.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: 4th or 5th intercostal space, just anterior to the mid-axillary line, without delay. Here, with the team leader able to do it, NICE recommends open thoracostomy followed by a chest drain. If that couldn't be done immediately, I'd needle-decompress at the same site rather than wait. A standard cannula in the 2nd space often doesn't reach the pleura.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Chest drain through the thoracostomy, then reassess. I'd watch for the tension coming back, and if the drain loses a lot of blood, that's a haemothorax and a thoracotomy conversation.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Major haemorrhage protocol. Tranexamic acid now: 40 minutes since injury, so well within 3 hours. Plasma and red cells 1:1, no crystalloid. I'd accept a lower pressure as long as he keeps a central pulse and mentation.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Transient or non-responder: minimal imaging, only what directs intervention, and damage control surgery. A negative FAST wouldn't reassure me. If he responds, whole-body CT.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Team leader, a summary: right tension decompressed, drain in, still shocked after two units, TXA given. I need the consultant surgeon and theatre alerted now.

failures.move: Removing the collar and blocks to examine the neck without manual in-line stabilisation.
failures.consequence: Safety-critical: risks converting an unstable cervical fracture into a cord injury.

failures.move: Waiting for a chest X-ray to confirm a tension pneumothorax in a shocked patient.
failures.consequence: Safety-critical: he can arrest while the film is taken.

failures.move: Decompressing medial to the mid-clavicular line or near the sternum.
failures.consequence: Safety-critical: risks injury to the heart and internal mammary vessels.

failures.move: Working through the survey silently, without telling the team leader.
failures.consequence: The team can't coordinate blood, theatre or imaging.

recovery.when: You went to the chest before the airway
recovery.line: Let me restart: <C>ABCDE, with the cervical spine held in line throughout.

recovery.when: You're asked for an X-ray first
recovery.line: He's hypoxic and hypotensive, so I'd decompress first and image afterwards.

knowledge.fact: <C>ABCDE with manual in-line cervical spine immobilisation, particularly during airway interventions.

Tension pneumothorax with haemodynamic instability or severe respiratory compromise: decompress without delay, before imaging (1.4.1). In hospital: open thoracostomy followed by a chest drain (1.4.2).
Needle decompression remains the alternative when open thoracostomy can't be done immediately; decompression must not wait.
Adult decompression site: 4th or 5th intercostal space, just anterior to the mid-axillary line. Children: 2nd space, mid-clavicular line.
Tranexamic acid as soon as possible; not more than 3 hours after injury unless hyperfibrinolysis. No crystalloid in active bleeding; plasma to red cells 1:1.
Tranexamic acid regimen: 1 g IV over 10 minutes, then 1 g over 8 hours.

recall.think: Tension pneumothorax and haemorrhage kill in minutes; a careless neck can paralyse.
recall.say: "Tension pneumothorax: I'm decompressing now, before any X-ray."
recall.trap: Waiting for tracheal deviation or an X-ray.
recall.finish: Chest drain, then CT if responding or damage control surgery if not.

sources.name: ICBSE Guide to the intercollegiate MRCS examination
sources.supports: Station format: 9 minutes with 1 minute's reading; examiner-led questioning in applied knowledge stations

sources.name: NICE NG39: Major trauma: assessment and initial management
sources.supports: In hospital: decompress a tension pneumothorax before imaging only if haemodynamic instability or severe respiratory compromise (1.4.1); open thoracostomy followed by a chest drain (1.4.2); observe for recurrence after decompression (1.3.6); IV tranexamic acid as soon as possible in active or suspected active bleeding (1.5.4), not more than 3 hours after injury unless hyperfibrinolysis (1.5.5); major haemorrhage protocol on physiology and response to volume (1.5.13); restrictive volume resuscitation until bleeding controlled, titrated to maintain central circulation (1.5.18, 1.5.20); no crystalloids in active bleeding in hospital (1.5.23); plasma to red cells 1:1 in adults (1.5.24); limit imaging in non-responders (1.5.29); immediate CT if responding (1.5.31); whole-body CT in blunt multiple injury (1.5.34); a negative FAST does not exclude intraperitoneal or retroperitoneal haemorrhage (1.5.30); damage control surgery for non-responders (1.5.37); a senior nurse or trauma team leader receives the pre-alert, and the trauma team leader is easily identifiable to receive the handover (1.8.4-1.8.5)

sources.name: NICE NG41: Spinal injury: assessment and initial management
sources.supports: <C>ABCDE: catastrophic haemorrhage, airway with in-line spinal immobilisation, breathing, circulation, disability, exposure (1.1.1); manual in-line immobilisation of the cervical spine at all stages, particularly during airway intervention (1.1.2)

sources.name: RCEMLearning reference: Thoracic trauma (Lloyd G; eds Kendall JM, McMorran S)
sources.supports: Tension pneumothorax: hypoxia early, hypotension late; tracheal deviation and hyper-resonance are soft signs; neck veins may not be distended in haemorrhagic shock; open thoracostomy then chest drain where expertise is available, needle decompression the alternative when this is not immediately possible; do not X-ray first, decompress then image; adult needle site now the 4th-5th intercostal space just anterior to the mid-axillary line (children still 2nd space mid-clavicular); finger thoracostomy at the same site; a 4.5 cm cannula may not reach the pleura via the 2nd space

sources.name: Ahmad SJS, Degiannis JR, et al. Meta-analysis of the optimal needle length and decompression site for tension pneumothorax and consensus recommendations on current ATLS and ETC guidelines. World J Emerg Surg 2025;20:39
sources.supports: Reports ATLS advice: 5 cm (small adults) or 8 cm needle at the 4th or 5th intercostal space in the anterior mid-axillary line; European Trauma Course: 2nd intercostal space mid-clavicular line

sources.name: CRASH-2 trial collaborators. Effects of tranexamic acid on death, vascular occlusive events, and blood transfusion in trauma patients with significant haemorrhage (CRASH-2). Lancet 2010;376:23–32
sources.supports: Tranexamic acid regimen: 1 g IV over 10 minutes, then 1 g over 8 hours

partner.opening: Mr Hale has just arrived. You're on the trauma team. Talk me through your assessment and management.

reveals.trigger: Asks about catastrophic haemorrhage and airway
reveals.finding: No external haemorrhage. He is talking in short phrases. Collar and blocks on.
Right side: reduced expansion, absent breath sounds, hyper-resonant. Trachea central. Neck veins not visible.
Rush of air. SpO2 rises to 93%, BP 94/58, pulse 120.
Five minutes later: BP 80/46, pulse 128, abdomen tender in the left upper quadrant, pelvis stable, binder on.
After two units of red cells and two of plasma: BP rises to 98/62, then falls to 82/48 within 10 minutes, pulse 126 (transient response).

push.question: Why not confirm the pneumothorax on X-ray first?
push.expect: He is unstable; NICE says decompress before imaging when there is haemodynamic instability or severe respiratory compromise.

push.question: Where and how would you decompress, and why there?
push.expect: 4th or 5th intercostal space just anterior to the mid-axillary line; open thoracostomy then drain with the expertise present, needle if that can't be done at once; thinner chest wall, away from the heart and great vessels.

push.question: When would you give tranexamic acid, and when not?
push.expect: As soon as possible with active or suspected bleeding; not beyond 3 hours unless hyperfibrinolysis.

curveballs.prompt: He arrived 4 hours after the crash. Tranexamic acid?
curveballs.safeAnswer: Not routinely beyond 3 hours after injury unless there is evidence of hyperfibrinolysis.

curveballs.prompt: After the drain his SpO2 falls again and he becomes more breathless and hypotensive.
curveballs.safeAnswer: Recurrent tension or a blocked or displaced drain: reassess, check the drain, and decompress again.

curveballs.prompt: The ED registrar wants to take the collar off to intubate.
curveballs.safeAnswer: Remove the front of the collar only with someone holding manual in-line stabilisation throughout.
